extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators and researchers (elementary grades 3–4); assessment specialists; curriculum developers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and comparison of third- and fourth-grade students' procedural (domain-free) writing and mathematical writing responses to scripted prompts, and implications for using written products to infer mathematical conceptual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between procedural writing and mathematical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The study examines the relationship between procedural writing and mathematical writing of third- and fourth-grade students, using separate prompt types (two 'domain-free' procedural prompts and three prompts requesting a response regarding a mathematical procedure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating student written products, distinguish whether the task is domain-free procedural writing or explicitly mathematical; prompt type is a key dimension that shapes the nature of responses and what they reveal about students' mathematical understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt type (domain-free vs mathematics-specific) as an evaluative factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Two prompts were 'domain-free' procedural writing prompts and three requested a response related to a mathematical procedure. Prompt design and domain-specific framing affect student responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and classify prompts clearly when using writing to assess math understanding. Compare responses by prompt type because domain-free procedural prompts may elicit different evidence about conceptual knowledge than math-specific prompts.

rubrics_metrics.name: General writing ability influences mathematical writing (number of words)
rubrics_metrics.description: A significant main effect of general writing ability on mathematical writing was recorded, based on the number of words students produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for students' general writing skills and verbosity when interpreting mathematical writing products: raw length (number of words) can confound inferences about mathematical understanding. Controlling for general writing ability or using measures beyond word count is advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints on using written products to reveal conceptual understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: There are factors which place constraints on the adequacy of written products to reveal the quality and degree of children's conceptual understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about treating written work as a direct indicator of conceptual understanding. Consider limitations such as writing ability, prompt suitability, and other contextual factors; use multiple evidence sources or adjusted interpretation methods when inferring mathematical knowledge from writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and inclusion criteria for valid comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Only responses of children whose parents indicated their approval and who were present for all of the writing samples were considered (study n=120; four classrooms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When collecting and analyzing student writing for assessment or research, apply consistent inclusion criteria (e.g., consent, complete data across conditions) to ensure validity of comparisons across prompt types and students.
